title: The laugh in Maya's hall
hookLine: Duryodhana is fooled by Maya's hall and laughed at, and a host's duty to a guest is broken
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god

cards: The guests have gone home, but one has stayed behind. Duryodhana lingers at Indraprastha with his uncle Shakuni, wandering through the great hall the asura builder Maya made for the Pandavas.
It's a hall of wonders, and wonders can be tricky. Floors that look like water. Water that looks like floor.
Doors that seem open and aren't. A new story starts here, the dice game. But it doesn't start with dice.
It starts with a man walking through a beautiful room and getting it wrong, again and again.

teach.b: In the telling, Duryodhana comes to a spot on the floor that looks like a pool. It's crystal, but he takes it for water and gathers up his clothes to wade across. Nothing wet.
Then he comes to a real pool, so clear it looks like solid floor, and walks straight in, clothes and all. Bhima sees it, and laughs. The servants laugh too.
Yudhishthira, the host, sends him dry clothes. By the end, the hall has fooled him over and over, and his mistakes have had an audience. Now, the teaching.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS A GOD.
teach.b: Hindu homes keep an old line, from the Taittiriya Upanishad: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you. That's why so many families meet a visitor with water, a seat, and far too much food.
In Maya's hall the line is tested. Yudhishthira keeps it: his guest is soaked, so he covers him. Bhima forgets it: his guest is soaked, so he laughs.

teach.h: THE WOUND OPENS BEFORE THE DICE.
teach.b: Many teachers read the moment this way: the dice game, and the war after it, open from a guest shamed in the house that should have sheltered him. The poem doesn't excuse what Duryodhana does next.
It shows where the wound opened. Today it's the same small test. Someone at your table spills, mispronounces a dish, walks into the wrong room.
Yudhishthira's way is to hand them the dry clothes before anyone gets to laugh.

how: Many Hindu homes still greet a guest with water, a seat and food, following atithi devo bhava; and some storytellers treat Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's hall as the opening of the dice-game story.

o: a hall of illusions built by an asura
a game of dice, played for stakes
a welcome of water for an honored guest

s: the dice game story begins with dice
it begins with Duryodhana fooled by Maya's hall and laughed at.
Duryodhana walked into a real pool he took for floor
the water was so clear it looked solid, and he fell in.
atithi devo bhava means the guest should honor the host
it's the other way round: let the guest be a god to you. the host serves.

games.q: you're the host. a guest in your house, one who has never wished you well, has just walked into your pool in full royal dress. what does atithi devo bhava ask of you?
o: cover him: send dry clothes, and let no one laugh.
games.why: the guest is a god in your house, even a difficult one. Yudhishthira sent dry clothes; Bhima laughed, and many teachers read that laugh as where the quarrel began.

practice: Picture someone coming to your door this week: a friend, a neighbor, someone you don't know well.
In your mind, do what Hindu homes have done for centuries: open the door, offer a glass of water, offer a seat, and let them feel like the most important person in the room.
Then remember one time a guest of yours was embarrassed, and see yourself handing them the dry clothes. If you pray, you can bring that guest into your prayer; if not, simply wish them ease.

wordCard.voice: Dyuta, the game of dice this story is named for. A story that doesn't begin with dice, but with a guest fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at as he falls.

orig.note: Sanskrit dyūta: dice play, gambling; the name of the section of the poem this story begins.

carryVoice: Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is god. Yudhishthira sent dry clothes; Bhima laughed. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duryodhana in Maya's hall: crystal taken for water, the pool, Bhima's laughter, the doors)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (atithi devo bhava, 'let the guest be a god to you', among the teacher's parting instructions)
